## `octelium`

```text
Octelium enables you to connect to Octelium Clusters, access and serve Services

Usage:
  octelium [command]

Available Commands:
  auth        Authentication-related operations to the Cluster
  config      Set Service Config
  connect     Connect to a Cluster
  cp          Copy files between the local filesystem and remote filesystems of connected Octelium sessions, or between two sessions
  daemon      Run the Octelium client daemon
  disconnect  Disconnect from the Cluster
  get
  login       Log in to a Cluster
  logout      Log out from a Cluster
  ssh         Open an SSH session to a connected Octelium session
  status      Show general information about User and Cluster
  version     Print version information

Flags:
      --domain string    The Cluster Domain
      --homedir string   Override Octelium home directory
      --logout           Log out after executing the command. This is useful when using commands such as "octelium connect" inside ephemeral environments such as containers
```

## `octelium connect`

```text
Connect to a Cluster

Usage:
  octelium connect [flags]

Examples:

# Connect to a Cluster
octelium connect
# OR via the detached mode in background
octelium connect -d

# Publish/map the Service svc1 to localhost:8080
octelium connect -p svc1:8080

# Publish multiple Services
octelium connect -p svc1:8080 -p svc2:3000 -p svc3:ns1:9090

# Publish the Service svc1 to 0.0.0.0:8080 of the host
octelium connect -p svc1:0.0.0.0:8080

# Serve the Service svc1
octelium connect --serve svc1
# Serve multiple Services
octelium connect --serve svc1 --serve svc2 --serve svc3.ns1
# Serve all available Services for the User
octelium connect --serve-all

# Serve embedded SSH Services
octelium connect --essh

# Connect with an Authentication Token
octelium connect --detach --auth-token <AUTHENTICATION_TOKEN>

# Connect using IPv4 only and skip using the Cluster DNS
octelium connect --ip-mode v4 --no-dns

Flags:
      --assertion string        Authenticate using assertion. Refer to the docs for more details.
      --auth-token string       Connect using an authentication Token without having to be logged in
  -d, --detach                  Run in the background
      --esocks5                 Run embedded SOCKS5 server
      --essh                    Enable serving SSH Services via embedded SSH
      --essh-user string        Force a host user to be used for eSSH sessions. This only works if Octelium is running as root
      --full-dns                Route all DNS queries to the Cluster DNS server instead of only the ones belonging to the Cluster domain.
                                This mode implicitly enables the local DNS server.
      --implementation string   Force implementation mode. Current values are "kernel" which is the kernel mode and currently works for WireGuard on Linux,
                                "tun" which is the TUN device mode and "gvisor" which is a pure userspace implementation. By default, Octelium would try
                                to find the best mode performance-wise and only resorts to the gvisor implementation if it does not have enough OS permissions.
      --ip-mode v4              Set the IP/Layer-3 networking mode. v4 for IPv4-only networking, `v6` for IPv6-only networking, `both` for both modes are valid
      --localdns                Enable local DNS server
      --localdns-addr string    Local DNS server listen address.
      --no-dns                  Skip setting the Cluster private DNS
  -p, --publish strings         Publish a Service to a host port. For example you can map the Service "svc1"
                                in the Namespace "ns1" to the host port "8080" as "svc1.ns1:8080".
                                For Services in the "default" Namespace you can simply use the format "service:port".
                                By default the listener host address is set to localhost. But you can explicitly set a specific listener address
                                in the format "service:host:port" (e.g. "svc1:0.0.0.0:8000", "svc1.ns1:0.0.0.0:8001")
      --scope strings
                                Scope is a way to limit the access to certain Services and Octelium APIs that works similarly to OAuth2.
                                This flag is used ONLY while authenticating using the --auth-token or --assertion flags.
                                You can use this flag also using the login subcommand.
                                For example, you can only limit the Session to access the Service "svc1.ns1" only using the scope "service:svc1.ns1"
                                You can also limit yourself to access only Services belonging to the Namespace "ns2" using the scope "service:ns2/*"
                                You can also use multiple scopes in the same command as follows "--scope service:svc1 --scope service:ns3/*"

      --serve strings           Select the service names assigned to this user to be served
      --serve-all               Serve all services assigned to the User
      --tunnel-mode string
                                	The tunneling mode for the  connection. The current available values are "wg", "wireguard" which use WireGuard (i.e. the default tunneling mode)
                                	and "quicv0" which uses QUIC. Currently "quicv0" is experimental and not suitable for production environments
```

## `octelium cp`

```text
Copy files or directories between the local filesystem and remote filesystems of connected Octelium sessions,
or between two sessions.

Session paths are specified as <session-name>:<path>.
You can list Session names via the "octeliumctl get sess" command.
Local paths are specified as plain filesystem paths.

Use -r to copy directories recursively.

Usage:
  octelium cp <source> <destination> [flags]

Examples:

  # Copy a local file to a session
  octelium cp ./config.json john-123456:/home/user/config.json

  # Copy a file from a session to local
  octelium cp john-123456:/home/user/output.csv ./output.csv

  # Copy a local directory to a session
  octelium cp -r ./src/ john-123456:/home/user/src/

  # Copy a directory from a session to local
  octelium cp -r john-123456:/home/user/dist/ ./dist/

  # Copy a file from one session to another
  octelium cp john-123456:/home/user/data.json linus-abcdef:/home/user/data.json

  # Copy a directory from one session to another
  octelium cp -r john-123456:/home/user/data/ linus-abcdef:/home/user/data/

Flags:
  -r, --recursive   Recursively copy directories
```

## `octelium daemon`

```text
Run the privileged Octelium client daemon which owns the authentication
credentials, the Connections and the host networking configuration of its owner
and which serves the local client API to the local frontends such as the
Octelium CLI itself and the Octelium desktop application.

The daemon is owned by a single OS user. The owner is either set via the --owner
flag or it is the OS user of the first local API caller.

Usage:
  octelium daemon [flags]

Examples:

# Run the Octelium daemon. It is normally run as an OS service as opposed to
# being run manually.
octelium daemon

# Run the daemon at a specific local API address and state directory
octelium daemon --listen /var/run/octelium/daemon.sock --state-dir /var/lib/octelium

# Run the daemon for a specific OS user
octelium daemon --owner 1000

Flags:
      --listen string      The address of the local API. This is the path of the Unix domain socket on
                           Linux and macOS and the name of the named pipe on Windows. By default the daemon
                           uses the standard address of the platform.
      --owner string       The ID of the OS user that owns this daemon. This is the UID on Linux and macOS
                           and the SID on Windows. The local API calls of every other OS user are rejected.
                           By default the daemon is owned by the OS user of the first local API caller.
      --state-dir string   The root directory of the daemon state. By default the daemon stores the
                           credentials and the settings of its owner in the standard Octelium home
                           directory of the owner which is the very same local state used by the Octelium
                           CLI. Setting this flag stores them in a sub-directory of it instead which makes
                           the daemon and the CLI of the owner use separate Cluster Sessions.
```

## `octelium login`

```text
Log in to a Cluster

Usage:
  octelium login [flags]

Examples:

octeliumctl login --auth-token <AUTHENTICATION_TOKEN>
octeliumctl login --domain octelium.example.com

Flags:
      --assertion string    Authenticate using an assertion. Refer to the docs for more details.
      --auth-token string   Authentication Token
      --scope strings
                            Scope is a way to limit the access to certain Services and Octelium APIs that works similarly to OAuth2.
                            This flag is used ONLY while authenticating using the --auth-token or --assertion flags.
                            You can use this flag also using the login subcommand.
                            For example, you can only limit the Session to access the Service "svc1.ns1" only using the scope "service:svc1.ns1"
                            You can also limit yourself to access only Services belonging to the Namespace "ns2" using the scope "service:ns2/*"
                            You can also use multiple scopes in the same command as follows "--scope service:svc1 --scope service:ns3/*"

      --web                 Authenticate using the web Portal
```

## `octelium ssh`

```text
Open an interactive SSH session or execute a remote command on a connected
Octelium Session using its name.

A remote command and its arguments can be passed after a double-dash (--).
If no command is given, an interactive shell is opened.

Usage:
  octelium ssh <session-name> [-- command [args...]] [flags]

Examples:

  # Open an interactive shell
  octelium ssh john-abcdef

  # Run a single remote command
  octelium ssh john-abcdef -- uptime

  # Run a shell pipeline
  octelium ssh john-abcdef -- sh -c "ps aux | grep python"

  # Local port forward: forward local :5432 to remote localhost:5432
  octelium ssh john-abcdef -L 5432:localhost:5432

  # Multiple port forwards, no interactive shell
  octelium ssh john-abcdef -N \
    -L 5432:localhost:5432 \
    -L 6379:localhost:6379

  # Dynamic SOCKS5 proxy on local port 1080
  octelium ssh john-abcdef -D 1080 -N

Flags:
  -D, --dynamic stringArray   Dynamic (SOCKS5) forward: [bind_addr:]port
  -L, --local stringArray     Local port forward: [bind_addr:]port:host:hostport
  -N, --no-command            Do not execute a remote command (useful for port forwarding only)
```
